passage:
Last March, Tejas's first spring in Guwahati: he still called Pune 'home' and Guwahati 'here,' and counted the days until Diwali leave.
This March, a Saturday: flying back from his cousin's wedding in Pune, his suitcase heavy with bakarwadi, Tejas caught himself saying on the phone, 'I'll be home by nine,' meaning his rented flat near the Brahmaputra. He smiled at that.
Monday, two days later: Hrithik, a new hire from Jaipur, sat at the next desk looking lost. At lunch Tejas walked him to the momo stall he loved, showed him which bus avoided the Beltola jam, and said, 'The third week is rough. Message me.' That evening Tejas sent a photo of the river to his mother in Pune and a photo of her kitchen to the office group. Both places, he thought, had made him.

qa.q: What was in Tejas's suitcase when he flew back from Pune?
Why did Tejas smile when he said 'I'll be home by nine'?
qa.a: He realised Guwahati had quietly become home too, and he felt surprised and warmed by it.

qa.q: How does Tejas use his own year to help Hrithik?
qa.a: He shares practical tips and warns that the third week is rough, inviting Hrithik to message him, which makes the start less lonely.

qa.q: What might Hrithik be feeling at lunch with Tejas?
qa.a: Hrithik, new and lost, probably feels relieved to have someone show the way and admit the hard weeks ahead.

grounding: Shows, across a year and two days, a person for whom home has become two places, who feels grateful to both and guides a newcomer.

passage: Payal, before you go, let your Indu maasi tell you one thing. When I moved to Singapore at twenty-five, I thought one day I'd have to choose, here or Kanpur. By the second year I stopped choosing. On Sunday mornings I bought kaya toast at the hawker centre with my neighbour, Mrs Tan, and on Sunday evenings I called your nani and heard every detail of the gali. I kept a jar of her aam ka achaar on my shelf and a pot of pandan on my windowsill. When a young nurse from Lucknow joined my ward and cried in the locker room in her first month, I took her to the hawker centre and told her it gets easier. It does. I'm grateful to both places, beta. Kanpur gave me my roots; Singapore gave me my spine. You'll carry two homes too, and still be only you.

qa.q: What did Indu keep on her windowsill?
What does Indu mean by 'Kanpur gave me my roots; Singapore gave me my spine'?
qa.a: She feels grateful to both: Kanpur gave her family and belonging, and Singapore made her strong and independent.

qa.q: How did Indu pass on what she had learned?
qa.a: She took the crying new nurse from Lucknow to the hawker centre and reassured her, helping a newcomer through the same path.

qa.q: How might Payal feel hearing this before leaving?
qa.a: Payal may feel reassured that moving does not mean losing home, and that Indu maasi understands what lies ahead.

grounding: Illustrates a person who, after moving, holds two homes with gratitude and helps a newcomer through the same path.
